title: The Scan Cycle in Practice: Order, Pulses and Last Write Wins
oneLiner: What the read, execute, write loop means for the code you write: inputs frozen for the whole scan, outputs written once at the end, statement order creating one-scan lags, and pulses too short to see.
keyTakeaway: The program sees a snapshot of the inputs and only its final output values reach the field. So write each output in one place, never wait inside a scan, and remember that anything computed below a statement reaches it one scan late.
explanation:
The earlier lesson PLCs: How They're Different From a Normal Computer introduced the scan cycle: read every input into memory, run the whole program top to bottom, write every output, do housekeeping, repeat. This lesson is about what that means when you write the program, because many surprising PLC bugs come from forgetting it.

Three consequences matter most. First, the program never sees a live input. It sees the input image, a snapshot taken at the start of the scan, so an input that changes mid-scan waits for the next scan, and a pulse shorter than a scan can be missed entirely. Second, outputs reach the real world only at the end of the scan, so if the program writes an output twice, only the last value counts. Third, the program runs in order, so a statement that reads a value computed further down sees last scan's value: a one-scan lag that is harmless until two pieces of logic depend on each other's timing.

That ordering is the PLC's version of a race condition. There are no threads fighting over memory in a single-task program like these, but the result can still depend on the order things happen in and on which scan a change lands in. A scan typically takes anywhere from under a millisecond to a few tens of milliseconds, depending on the controller and the size of the program.

Step through the scan below one phase at a time, then try the statement order, last-write and one-scan pulse examples.
